hfaqs.a: No. Start with spoken Urdu in Roman letters, and let the script come second. Learners who speak first stay motivated far longer than learners who drill letters for a month before saying a word.
hfaqs.q: Must I learn the Urdu script before speaking?

hfaqs.a: السلام علیکم for respect, ہاں and نہیں, شکریہ, معاف کیجیے, ٹھیک ہے, and میں — I. With those seven you can open any interaction politely while your vocabulary grows underneath.
hfaqs.q: Which words should I learn in week one?

hfaqs.a: The retroflexes and Persian-Arabic sounds — ع غ ق خ — plus reading right-to-left. Ten minutes of daily listening retunes your ears within weeks; the pronunciation page walks you through each one.
hfaqs.q: What is the hardest part of Urdu?

how.d: Short, plain-English explanations — no grammar walls, no jargon without a translation.
Each phrase speaks in a native Urdu voice. Slow it to 0.2× and repeat until it sticks.
Every topic ends in practice: quiz yourself, then review the words until they stay.

title: Urdu

topics.desc: السلام علیکم and beyond — greet with warmth from your first word. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: السلام علیکم with hand on heart — respectful everywhere. Casual ہیلو works with friends; السلام علیکم never fails.
faqs.q: How do I say hello respectfully?

faqs.a: آپ کیسے ہیں؟ (formal) or تم کیسے ہو؟ (informal) — and answer میں ٹھیک ہوں، شکریہ (I'm fine, thanks). Health-questions open hearts.
faqs.q: How do I ask how someone is?

faqs.a: صبح بخیر (good morning), شب بخیر (good night), آداب (respectful greeting). Time-greetings show care; use them generously.

topics.lede: السلام علیکم and beyond — greet with warmth from your first word.
topics.note: A note on السلام علیکم. السلام علیکم (assalam-o-alaikum — peace be upon you) carries a hand on the heart and genuine warmth — the universal key. Answer وعلیکم السلام (and upon you be peace). Respect first, everything else follows.
paras: Greetings open every door: السلام علیکم (respectful hello), آداب (courteous hello), ہیلو (casual hi). Hand on heart, say السلام علیکم, and doors open — bazaars, offices, homes. One phrase, infinite welcome.

Health-questions show you care: آپ کیسے ہیں؟ (how are you, formal), میں ٹھیک ہوں (I'm fine), اور آپ؟ (and you?). Urdu small talk runs on genuine enquiry — ask properly, listen properly, belong quickly.
Time splits the day: صبح بخیر (good morning), شب بخیر (good night). Morning greetings before noon, شب بخیر only at parting — timing your بخیر shows cultural fluency.

Partings promise return: خدا حافظ (goodbye), پھر ملیں گے (we'll meet again), اپنا خیال رکھیے (take care). Rarely goodbye without a next meeting — پھر ملیں گے assumes friendship continues. Say it warmly; mean it always.
topics.title: Saying hello the Urdu way

topics.desc: ا ب پ to ی ے — the Perso-Arabic alphabet, right-to-left, made friendly. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: 39 letters — Arabic's set plus پ چ ٹ ڈ ڑ ژ ں ے and more. Same right-to-left flow, extra Indo-Persian sounds.
Almost all letters join within words — initial, middle, final shapes. Practice joining early; reading flows from writing.
The vowel-bearers ا آ ع plus ب پ ت ٹ — then ج چ ح خ. Sounds before shapes; reading follows speaking.

topics.lede: ا ب پ to ی ے — the Perso-Arabic alphabet, right-to-left, made friendly.

links.desc: Letters from zero, step by step.
links.label: Urdu basics

topics.note: A note on right-to-left. Urdu flows right-to-left — start at the right edge and glide leftwards. ا ب پ ت reads a-ba-pa-ta. Eyes adjust within days; soon left-to-right scripts feel backwards.
paras: Vowels anchor everything: ا آ (a/aa), ع (i/e carrier), ے (e), و (o/u carrier). Long-short pairs matter — دل (heart) vs دیل differs by dots and shape. Chant letters in order daily; the mouth memorises what the ear repeats.

Consonants march in families: ب پ ت ٹ (lips-teeth), ج چ ح خ (throat-palate), د ڈ ذ ر ڑ (tongue-tip), س ش ص ز (hissers). Family by family, feel where each sound lives — Urdu pronunciation is geography you can touch.
Special letters crown the set: ع غ ق (deep throat), خ (guttural kh), ژ (Persian zh), ں (nasal noon). خبر (news) shows خ in action; عشق (love) shows ع. Special letters, everyday words.
Joining grids it all: ب + ا = با, م + ی + ں = میں — letters melt into words. Write joining drills daily; reading unlocks when hands know the shapes. Script becomes a friend for life.
topics.title: Urdu alphabet

topics.desc: ایک دو تین to سو — count, pay and bargain in Urdu. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: ایک دو تین چار پانچ چھ سات آٹھ نو دس — chant to ten, then گیارہ بارہ تیرہ to twenty. Rhythm first, precision follows.
بیس (20), تیس (30), چالیس (40), پچاس (50) — then combine: اکیس (21), بتیس (32). Tens plus units, endlessly.
سو (100), ہزار (1000), لاکھ (100,000). کتنے؟ (how many?) asks; numbers answer. Markets run on these three.

topics.lede: ایک دو تین to سو — count, pay and bargain in Urdu.
topics.note: A note on کتنے؟ کتنے؟ (kitne — how much / how many?) is the most useful question — کتنے روپے؟ (how many rupees?), کتنے بجے؟ (what time is it?). One word, every transaction. Ask کتنے fearlessly; numbers come to you.
paras: One to ten sings: ایک دو تین چار پانچ چھ سات آٹھ نو دس — chant it walking, cooking, waiting. Urdu numbers love rhythm; your tongue learns faster than your brain. Ten numbers, total freedom in every shop.
Teens climb steadily: گیارہ بارہ تیرہ چودہ پندرہ سولہ سترہ اٹھارہ انیس بیس — eleven to twenty. انیس (19) and بیس (20) open the tens; climb daily and teens become trivial.
Tens multiply power: بیس تیس چالیس پچاس ساٹھ ستر اسی نوے سو — 20 to 100. Combine freely: اکیس (21), پچیس (25), ستائیس (27) — the tongue-twisters that prove fluency.
Hundreds rule markets: سو (100), دو سو (200), ہزار (1000), لاکھ (100,000). ڈیڑھ سو (150) and اڑھائی سو (250) charm shopkeepers — halves and quarters in pure Urdu. Money talks; count it in Urdu.
topics.title: Counting in Urdu

topics.desc: میں, آپ, ہاں, نہیں — hold your first real Urdu conversations. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: آپ کا نام کیا ہے؟ (what's your name?) — answer میرا نام راہل ہے (my name is Rahul). Names first, friendship follows.
faqs.q: How do I ask someone's name?

faqs.a: ہاں (yes), نہیں (no) — short, clear, universal. جی ہاں adds respect; نا is casual. Yes-no fluency first.
مجھے سمجھ نہیں آیا (I didn't understand) and آہستہ بولیے (please speak slowly). Honesty tunes every speaker to your level.

topics.lede: میں, آپ, ہاں, نہیں — hold your first real Urdu conversations.

links.desc: Dialogues with audio, step by step.
links.label: Urdu conversation lessons

topics.note: A note on مجھے. مجھے (mujhe — to-me) is Urdu's magic word — مجھے چاہیے (I want), مجھے سمجھ آیا (I understood), مجھے معلوم ہے (I know). Experiences flow TOWARD you in Urdu; master مجھے and fifty sentences unlock.
paras: People anchor talk: میں (I), آپ (you formal), وہ (he/she/they). میں اردو سیکھتا ہوں (I'm learning Urdu) — gender shows on verbs, proudly. Introduce yourself; conversations ignite.
Questions drive dialogue: کیا؟ (what?), کہاں؟ (where?), کب؟ (when?), کیوں؟ (why?), کیسے؟ (how?). آپ کہاں رہتے ہیں؟ (where do you live?) — one question word plus any verb equals conversation.
Politeness oils everything: براہ کرم (please) and معاف کیجیے (sorry/excuse me). معاف کیجیے، آہستہ بولیے (sorry, speak slowly) — apologies plus requests, the learner's armour.
Repair keeps talk alive: مجھے سمجھ نہیں آیا (I didn't understand), پھر کہیے (please say again), اس کا مطلب کیا ہے؟ (what does this mean?). Broken Urdu beats silent perfection — stumble forward daily.
topics.title: Real Urdu conversation

topics.desc: ہے, جانا, کرنا — the verbs that carry every Urdu sentence. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: میں ہوں (I am), تم ہو, وہ ہے, ہم ہیں, آپ ہیں, وہ ہیں. Being first, everything else after.
Present uses root + تا/تی/تے + ہے: میں کرتا ہوں (I do, m), میں کرتی ہوں (f). Gender shows on every present verb.
faqs.q: How does the present tense work?

faqs.a: جانا (to go), آنا (to come), کرنا (to do), کھانا (to eat), بولنا (to speak). Five verbs, half of daily speech.

topics.lede: ہے, جانا, کرنا — the verbs that carry every Urdu sentence.
topics.note: A note on ہوں/ہے/ہیں. The ہوں family (hun/hai/hain) is Urdu's heartbeat — میں ہوں (I am), وہ ہے (he/she is), آپ ہیں (you are). Every present-tense sentence pulses with ہ. Learn this family cold; the whole tense follows.
paras: Being grounds all: ہوں/ہے (am/is/are) — میں ہوں (I am), ہم ہیں (we are), آپ ہیں (you are), وہ ہیں (they are). ہے anchors identity, place, state — میں یہاں ہوں (I'm here), میں ٹھیک ہوں (I'm fine). Be first.
Going and coming move life: جانا (to go), آنا (to come) — میں جاتا ہوں (I go), میں آتا ہوں (I come). Direction verbs plus کہاں (where) navigate everywhere — میں لاہور جاتا ہوں (I'm going to Lahore).
Doing and eating fill days: کرنا (to do), کھانا (to eat), پینا (to drink) — میں کام کرتا ہوں (I work), میں کھاتا ہوں (I eat). Daily verbs, daily use; conjugate them in your sleep.
Speaking and knowing crown all: بولنا (to speak), پڑھنا (to read), لکھنا (to write) — میں اردو بولتا ہوں (I speak Urdu). Say it now, imperfectly; say it daily until the mirror agrees.
topics.title: Urdu verbs

topics.desc: پانی, گھر, کام, پیار — the hundred words Urdu daily life runs on. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Body, home, food, people: پانی (water), گھر (house), ماں (mother), دوست (friend). Concrete nouns first — point, name, own.
Adjectives agree with gender: اچھا (good-m), اچھی (f). Learn pairs together — agreement becomes music.
آج (today), کل (tomorrow), گذشتہ کل (yesterday), اب (now). Time words frame every plan — learn them this week.

topics.lede: پانی, گھر, کام, پیار — the words Urdu daily life runs on.

links.desc: Words in course order, with drills.
links.label: Urdu vocabulary

topics.note: A note on خوب. خوب (khoob — nice/great) is the universal praise — خوب ہے (it's nice), بہت خوب (very nice). Food, films, friends' work — praise everything. Generous خوب earns generous friendship.
paras: Survival nouns anchor reality: پانی (water), کھانا (food), گھر (house), راستہ (road). Point at each, say it aloud, use it today — پانی چاہیے (I want water). Concrete first, abstract later.
People words warm speech: آدمی (person), دوست (friend), ماں (mother), بچہ (child). میرا دوست (my friend) introduces proudly; ماں calls home. People before things, always.
Describing words add colour: بڑا (big), چھوٹا (small), اچھا (good), نیا (new). Adjectives dance with gender — بڑا بھائی (big brother), بڑی بہن (big sister). Pair-learn each one.
Time and feeling complete the core: آج (today), پیار (love), خوشی (joy), کام (work). آج بہت کام ہے (there's lots of work today) — then پیار اور خوشی balance it. Words for living, not just talking.
topics.title: Core Urdu vocabulary

topics.desc: بریانی to کھیر — order, eat and praise food in Urdu. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: کھانا (meal), ناشتہ (breakfast), چائے (tea). مجھے بھوک لگی ہے (I'm hungry) opens every food conversation.
faqs.q: How do I talk about meals?

faqs.a: یہ کیا ہے؟ (what is this?) and مجھے بریانی چاہیے (I want biryani). Point, ask, order — menus fear the curious.
تیز (spicy), میٹھا (sweet), نمکین (salty), کھٹا (sour). کم تیز (less spicy) saves sensitive tongues.

topics.lede: بریانی to کھیر — order, eat and praise food in Urdu.
topics.note: A note on دسترخوان. دسترخوان (dastarkhwan — the spread meal-cloth) is hospitality itself — کھانا تیار ہے (food is ready) gathers everyone. مہمان نوازی (hospitality) is sacred; guests eat first, hosts eat joy. Food is love, served hot.
paras: Meals structure the day: ناشتہ (breakfast), کھانا (lunch/dinner), چائے (tea). چائے پییں گے؟ (shall we have tea?) — life runs on doodh-patti and conversation. Accept every cup; refuse nothing twice.

Ordering is easy bravery: مجھے ایک چائے چاہیے (I want one tea), بل دیجیے (please give the bill). ایک پلیٹ بریانی دیجیے (give one plate of biryani) — order the soul of the cuisine in Urdu. Dhabas reward attempts with extra raita.

Staples fill the dastarkhwan: چاول (rice), روٹی (flatbread), دال (lentils), سبزی (vegetables). سبزی کیا ہے؟ (what's the vegetable dish?) — ask daily, eat variously. Shared eating teaches vocabulary with every bite.
Tastes tune the tongue: تیز (spicy), میٹھا (sweet) — کھیر (rice pudding) crowns feasts. کم تیز کیجیے (make it less spicy) — then بہت خوب! (very nice!). Praise the cook; second helpings follow.
topics.title: Food phrases

topics.desc: ع غ ق خ, retroflexes, poetic rhythm — speak Urdu like a native. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Deep-throat sounds: ع (voiced squeeze), غ (gargled g), ق (deep k), خ (guttural kh). Listen to newsreaders; imitate slowly. Months of music in four letters.
faqs.q: How do I pronounce ع غ ق خ?

faqs.a: ٹ ڈ ڑ — tongue curls to the roof. ٹماٹر (tomato), ڈاک (post), پڑھنا (to read). Flap them boldly; Urdu retroflexes are proud.
Long-short pairs change words. Hold long vowels fully double — Urdu ears measure length precisely.

topics.lede: ع غ ق خ, retroflexes, poetic rhythm — speak Urdu like a native.
topics.note: A note on آہستہ. آہستہ (aahistaa — slowly) is the learner's best friend — آہستہ بولیے (please speak slowly). Say it with a smile and every Urdu speaker shifts to teacher-mode. Slow speech is kind speech; ask for it freely.
paras: The deep quartet rules: عشق (love), غم (sorrow), قلم (pen), خبر (news) — throat engaged, sound resonant. Minimal pairs drill them: کال (famine) vs قال (he said) — practise قلم vs کلم daily. Master these and Urdu voices beam.
Retroflexes flap boldly: ٹماٹر (tomato), ڈاک (post), پڑھنا (to read) — tongue back, tap forward. Urdu retroflexes hit harder than Hindi's; lean into them. Bold flaps mark the insider.
Length carries meaning: short and long vowels are different letters, different words. Double the long ones fully; clip the short ones crisp. Ears measure; mouths must comply.

Rhythm ties it together: آہستہ (slowly) first, then natural speed; زور سے (loudly) for clarity, خاموش (quiet) for calm. تلفظ (pronunciation) improves with echoing — shadow newsreaders daily, record yourself weekly.
topics.title: Urdu pronunciation

topics.desc: Two genders, postpositions, verb-final order — grammar without tears. Free, no sign-up.

faqs.a: Masculine and feminine — nouns, adjectives AND verbs agree. اچھا/اچھی (good), جاتا/جاتی (go). Pairs everywhere; learn them as sets.
کو marks direction (لاہور کو — to Lahore), نے marks doers (رام نے کیا — Ram did), سے means with/from. Postpositions follow nouns — learn each with ten examples.
Subject-Object-Verb: میں چاول کھاتا ہوں (I rice eat). Verb last, always. English order is the classic beginner error.

topics.lede: Two genders, postpositions, verb-final order — grammar without tears.
topics.note: A note on نے. نے (ne) marks the doer in past tense — رام نے کیا (Ram did), میں نے کھایا (I ate). Ergative, elegant, everywhere in stories. Tiny suffix, enormous workload.
paras: Two genders shape everything: masculine (لڑکا — boy), feminine (لڑکی — girl). Adjectives pair — اچھا/اچھی — and verbs pair too. Gender is not decoration; it is Urdu's skeleton.

Pronouns simplify persons: میں (I), تم (you-informal), آپ (you-formal), وہ (he-she/they), ہم (we). ہم vs ہم سب (we vs all-of-us) shades meaning; آپ is always plural-form, always respectful. Choose your you wisely.
Postpositions replace prepositions: -کو (to), -نے (by/doer), -سے (with/from), -میں (in). گھر کو جاؤ (go home), چمچ سے کھاؤ (eat with a spoon). Suffixes after nouns — think backwards from English.

Verbs anchor sentences last: میں چاول کھاتا ہوں (I rice eat), وہ اسکول جاتی ہے (she to-school goes). Present (کھاتا ہوں), past (کھایا), future (کھاؤں گا) — tense on verbs, time words framing. Verb-final: the one rule that never breaks.
